name: Adaptive Reuse
summary: Old buildings given a new use. Scarpa, Aulenti and Herzog and de Meuron keep the shell of a castle, station or power plant, and add a clear new layer that tells old from new.

philosophy.core_thesis: An existing building has value in its fabric and its memory, so keep it, change its use and let the new work be clearly new beside the old.
design_principles: Keep the existing structure and shell, and record its condition before you plan the new use.
Show the old and the new as two layers, with a gap or a joint of 20 to 100mm between them.
Choose a new material that contrasts with the old in tone and finish: glass, steel, or pale timber against brick and stone.
Keep the big old volume, such as a hall, a nave or a turbine hall of 10 to 35m, and insert new floors inside it.
Cut new openings only where the use needs them, and frame them so the old wall stays readable.
Leave marks of the former use on show, such as rails, stains, crane beams and chimneys.
anti_patterns: A complete demolition behind a retained front
A fake historical copy that blurs old and new
New work in the same material and style as the old
Covering the old fabric with thick cladding
A new use that needs the walls to be gutted
A sealed insertion that does not touch the old

massing.form: The existing building stays as the main mass, and a new roof, stair or inserted volume sits inside or on top of it.
massing.proportion: The original proportions, often a tall hall of 10 to 35m, are kept, with 20 to 40% new floor area.
massing.roof: The old roof is kept or repaired, and a new lightweight addition of glass or steel rises 1 to 3 storeys on it.
massing.relation_to_ground: The old plinth and ground relation are kept, and a new entrance or ramp is added.

structure.system: The old masonry, steel or concrete frame is kept, and a new steel or timber frame is added.
structure.span_and_module: The old module of 4 to 10m is kept; new floors span 6 to 12m; the new frame stands 20 to 100mm clear of the old.
structure.expression: The old and new structures read as two layers, and a joint, a reveal or a bracket tells them apart.

materials.finish: Layered and honest: patinated old brick and stone next to clean steel, glass and pale timber.

facade.composition: The old facade stays as it was; the new openings and the new layer are set in it and framed clearly.
facade.openings: Old openings are kept and new ones are cut; the window-to-wall ratio is 20 to 45%.

light_and_space.daylight: The old tall windows and roof lights bring in light, and the new glass inserts bring it deep into the plan.
light_and_space.spatial_sequence: A grand old hall, a new stair or bridge across it, then rooms of the new use.
light_and_space.interior_character: A ceiling of 4 to 20m with old trusses and crane beams, exposed brick, and new floors and light fittings.

ornament.attitude: The marks of use and age are the ornament: patina, scars and old fittings, and the new layer stays plain.

rules.rule: Set clean new steel and glass against old brick and stone.
Hold a gap or a reveal between the old fabric and the new.
Keep the old hall and set the human new floors inside it.
Make one new insertion, such as a stair, a bridge or a roof, the focus.
Keep the long view down the old hall open.
Lead the visitor through the old threshold into a new route.

emotion.target_response: Respect and curiosity: the viewer feels the memory of the old building and the energy of its new life.

use_cases: housing and offices from old factories
avoid_when: The site is empty and the brief asks for a new landmark.
The old fabric is unsafe and cannot be kept.

modifiers.how: Strip the finishes back to brick, steel and concrete, and show the old services.
Make the new layer a light steel and glass frame with exposed services.

positive: clear joint between old and new

canonical_works.work: Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa, Cape Town

sources.title: Liliane Wong, Adaptive Reuse: Extending the Lives of Buildings (Birkhäuser, 2017)
